title: The forgotten Forever War
gist: Despite being America's longest war, Afghanistan has left a strikingly thin political and cultural legacy compared with Vietnam, because the all-volunteer military, debt-financed spending and lack of ideological stakes insulated the American public from its costs — and five years on, this has produced only an aversion to ground troops, not to intervention itself.

themes.theme: Vietnam vs Afghanistan: parallel collapses, divergent legacies

insights.claim: Both the fall of South Vietnam (1975) and the fall of the Afghan Republic (2021) were preceded by US intelligence overestimating the client state's durability: Saigon was expected to hold a foothold until early 1976, and the Afghan Republic was expected to survive six to twelve months post-withdrawal — instead it collapsed before the US withdrawal was even complete.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: A recurring US intelligence failure pattern — systematically overestimating the durability of client governments before a withdrawal — worth weighing when assessing current US assessments of allied-state resilience elsewhere.
insights.quote: as late as March 1975, roughly a month before South Vietnam surrendered, US intelligence thought it possible that the besieged government in Saigon could retain a foothold in the south and resist total defeat until early 1976
insights.locator: Third paragraph, on US overestimation of client-state durability

insights.claim: Despite comparable scale — 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam versus roughly 2.77 million in Afghanistan and Iraq combined — the Vietnam War produced a decades-long cultural and political reckoning (major films, novels, the contested Vietnam memorial, the 'Vietnam Syndrome'), while Afghanistan has left a comparatively sparse legacy.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Central thesis of the piece: a war's scale doesn't determine its lasting political/cultural footprint — the structure of who bears its costs does, which matters for gauging how durably any future conflict will shape US politics.
insights.quote: It is therefore striking, five years later, how the legacies of the two wars have diverged.

insights.claim: Afghanistan was described by one account as the 'least reported war since at least WWI'; in 2010, it accounted for just 4% of US news coverage (Iraq only 1%), and no more than one in ten Americans named either conflict as their top news story.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Quantifies how thin the domestic information environment was around America's longest war, helping explain the shallow political salience of the withdrawal outcome.
insights.quote: By one account, Afghanistan was the ‘least reported war since at least WWI’.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'By the end of the decade'

insights.claim: A 2023 poll found more than four in ten Americans were unaware the Taliban had retaken control of Afghanistan, and over a third had not heard of the Taliban's growing restrictions on Afghan women.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Evidence of near-total public disengagement from a major foreign-policy outcome within two years, indicating low domestic political cost/accountability risk for policymakers on Afghanistan specifically.
insights.quote: One poll from 2023 showed that more than four in ten Americans were unaware of the Taliban retaking control of Afghanistan, while over a third had not heard of the Taliban’s growing restrictions on Afghan women.
insights.locator: Paragraph on Afghanistan disappearing from public consciousness

themes.theme: How the volunteer military and debt financing insulated the public

insights.claim: The US ended the draft in 1973 in response to Vietnam and shifted to an all-volunteer professional military, which narrowed the segment of society bearing combat burden and relied on repeated deployments of the same individuals — by 2008 many active-duty soldiers were on their second or third tours.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Structural explanation for why post-draft wars generate less domestic political backlash: the cost is concentrated on a narrow professional class rather than broadly shared, reducing the electoral salience of prolonged conflict.
insights.quote: By 2008, many active-duty soldiers were already on their second or third tours.
insights.locator: Paragraph on the end of the compulsory draft

insights.claim: Defence spending during the Vietnam era ran at 8–10% of GDP and was partly financed by a temporary 10% income-tax surcharge (1968); by contrast, Iraq/Afghanistan-era defence spending hovered around 4% of GDP and was financed mostly through borrowing rather than direct taxation.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that the shift from tax-financed to debt-financed war spending removed a visible economic sacrifice that once forced public engagement with war costs — a template for assessing how future US conflicts will be politically absorbed depending on financing method.
insights.quote: By contrast, during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, defence spending hovered around four per cent of GDP, mostly financed by borrowing.
insights.locator: Paragraph on Vietnam's visible economic sacrifices

insights.claim: Post-Vietnam military reforms included professionalising reserves, growing reliance on private contractors, and a shift toward 'risk-transfer militarism' — a mode of engagement using tools like drone warfare to keep coalition casualties minimal.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Names a specific doctrinal shift (Martin Shaw's 'risk-transfer militarism') useful as a lens for evaluating how low-casualty tools like drones structurally reduce domestic political constraints on future US military engagement.
insights.quote: a shift towards what Martin Shaw has described as ‘risk-transfer militarism’: a more targeted mode of engagement that kept coalition casualties to a minimum, not least through advancements in drone warfare

insights.claim: The Afghanistan War's total cost is estimated at $2.3 trillion, yet few Americans believed it was worth the enormous costs even though most did not consider it an outright mistake.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: A concrete fiscal benchmark for the total price tag of a two-decade counterinsurgency campaign, useful for scaling the cost of any future comparable engagement.
insights.quote: Few believed it was worth the enormous costs, which accumulated to an estimated $2.3 trillion.
insights.locator: Paragraph on the pessimistic but resigned public mood

themes.theme: No ideological defeat, no geopolitical windfall for rivals

insights.claim: Unlike Vietnam, where US defeat represented a direct ideological victory for a rival superpower, the Afghanistan withdrawal carried no comparable ideological defeat, since the Taliban's form of government had little appeal outside its own borders.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Explains why the Afghanistan withdrawal, despite its chaos, did not trigger a Vietnam-style national identity crisis — a useful causal factor for gauging how much domestic political fallout follows any future US disengagement.
insights.quote: there was no comparable ideological defeat, as the Taliban’s draconian form of government had little appeal outside its borders.
insights.locator: Paragraph on moving on from the war being psychologically easier

insights.claim: Although the fall of Kabul damaged US prestige across 24 surveyed countries, there was no corresponding increase in favourability toward rivals like China or Russia, indicating the withdrawal did not translate into a geopolitical win for US adversaries.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Counters the assumption that US setbacks automatically accrue to rival powers — a useful check on overly mechanical 'US decline = China/Russia gain' narratives in geopolitical positioning.
insights.quote: While the fall of Kabul may have damaged US prestige across 24 countries, there was no corresponding bump in favourability towards rivals like China or Russia.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Nor, as many initially feared'

insights.claim: Some US allies, including South Korea and Taiwan, viewed the Afghanistan withdrawal not as concerning but as a possible opportunity, believing it could free up more US resources for deployment elsewhere (implicitly, the Indo-Pacific).
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Suggests Indo-Pacific-facing allies read the Afghanistan exit as a resource-reallocation signal in their favour — relevant context for assessing regional alliance sentiment toward continued US force posture shifts toward China-facing theatres.
insights.quote: some, like South Korea and Taiwan, viewed it as a possible opportunity, believing it could free up more resources to be deployed elsewhere
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Nor, as many initially feared'

insights.claim: About 70% of the American public supported the decision to withdraw from Afghanistan by summer 2021, and subsequent criticism focused almost entirely on the execution of the withdrawal rather than the underlying strategic decision.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Shows the withdrawal decision itself had durable bipartisan public support, meaning the chaotic execution generated embarrassment but not a lasting political mandate against disengagement as such.
insights.quote: by summer 2021, about 70 per cent of the public supported the decision to withdraw, even if there was widespread concern about the plight of individual Afghans, such as military translators and human rights activists.
insights.locator: Paragraph on the bipartisan decision to withdraw

insights.claim: Unlike Vietnam Syndrome, which produced a broad reluctance to commit US troops abroad for decades, any 'Afghanistan Syndrome' has not reduced America's willingness to flex military muscle abroad (citing Ukraine, Venezuela, Iran) — it has produced only an aversion to putting large numbers of American boots on the ground.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Key actionable takeaway: expect continued US willingness to use air power, sanctions, proxies and limited strikes across multiple theatres, but strong political resistance to any large-scale ground troop commitment — a template for assessing escalation risk in Ukraine, Venezuela or Iran scenarios.
insights.quote: In terms of a willingness to flex its military muscle abroad – in Ukraine, in Venezuela, in Iran – America is as active as ever.

insights.claim: The Vietnam War left America with an identity crisis that took decades to resolve, while the Afghanistan withdrawal 'ended with a collective shrug,' with the public having largely moved on by the time the last soldier left.
insights.speaker: Jasmine Bhatia
insights.so_what: Summary framing for why Afghanistan carries far less enduring domestic political risk than its scale and duration would suggest — useful baseline for comparing the expected political durability of any future prolonged US military engagement.
insights.quote: The trauma of Vietnam left America with an identity crisis, one that took decades to resolve, if indeed it ever did. The Forever War ended with a collective shrug.
